Lecture 20

Gaussian random vectors

Deck C, slides 9 to 19 · 38 min read · 9 practice problems

Solutions stay collapsed until you click them.

Where we are. The normal is the most important single distribution (the CLT in L18 is the reason). This lecture builds its vector version, the multivariate Gaussian N(μ,Σ). Honestly, the whole lecture comes from one idea:

every Gaussian vector is an affine function of independent standard normals:  X=AZ+μ.

Combine that with the L19 tools (CAX+b​=ACX​AT and the Jacobian), and out comes everything: the density, the fact that linear maps keep vectors Gaussian, and the two properties that make Gaussians so nice to work with: marginals and conditionals of a Gaussian vector are Gaussian again, with explicit formulas.

Part A: the slides

Slide 9/36: Recap

On the slide. We looked at n-length random vectors X, which are essentially multivariate random variables. Its CDF/pdf is simply the joint CDF/pdf of the components. E[X]=[E[X1​],…,E[Xn​]], and CX​ is the covariance matrix. Let Y=G(X) where G:Rn→Rn is continuous and invertible with continuous partial derivatives. Let H denote its inverse. Then fY​(y)=fX​(H(y))∣J∣ where J is the determinant of the Jacobian matrix. If Y=AX+b, then CY​=ACX​AT and

fY​(y)=∣det(A)∣1​fX​(A−1(y−b)).

All proved in L19 (slides 4, 7 and 8). Keep an eye on the last formula: it's the engine of this lecture. We'll plug in a standard normal vector for X and see what comes out.

Slide 10/36: The standard normal vector

On the slide. An n-length random vector Z is called a standard normal vector if its components Zi​ are independent and standard normal. What is E[Z] and CZ​? Show that the pdf is given by

fZ​(z)=(2π)n/21​e−21​zTz.

This is the simplest Gaussian vector, the building block for all the others.

The blue question. Each Zi​ has mean 0 and variance 1, and independent components have zero covariance. So

E[Z]=0,CZ​=In​  (the n×n identity).

The pdf. Independent means the densities multiply, and multiplying exponentials adds the exponents:

fZ​(z)=i=1∏n​2π​1​e−zi2​/2=(2π)n/21​exp(−21​i=1∑n​zi2​)=(2π)n/21​e−21​zTz,

since zTz=z12​+⋯+zn2​=∥z∥2.

Worth noticing. fZ​ only depends on the length ∥z∥, not the direction. So the density looks the same in every direction, and rotating a standard normal vector gives a standard normal vector again. (If Q is orthogonal, QQT=I, then QZ has covariance QIQT=I, and by slide 14 it's Gaussian, so it's standard normal.)

Slide 11/36: Building general Gaussians from Z

On the slide. Now suppose X=AZ+μ. What is E[X] and CX​? E[X]=μ and CX​=AAT. Note that A can have dimension n×l, in which case Z is an l-length standard normal. What is fX​(x)?

The idea: take independent standard normals, mix them with a matrix A, shift by μ. Mixing creates correlations.

Mean and covariance. Straight from L19 slides 2 and 4:

E[X]=AE[Z]+μ=μ,CX​=ACZ​AT=AIAT=AAT.

The shape of A. A doesn't have to be square.

  • l<n (fewer sources of randomness than components). Then CX​=AAT has rank at most l<n, so it's singular. X is stuck on a lower-dimensional flat piece of Rn, and has no joint pdf. Example: X=(Z,2Z) always lies on the line x2​=2x1​. A line has zero area, so there's no density on the plane. It's still a perfectly good Gaussian vector, just a degenerate one. Last year's HW9 Q4 and Q6 (Part B) produce these.
  • l=n with A invertible: the usual case, with a pdf (next slide).

Slide 12/36: The multivariate Gaussian density

On the slide. What is fX​(x)?

fX​(x)=∣det(A)∣1​fZ​(A−1(x−μ))=(2π)n/2det(CX​)​1​e−21​(x−μ)TCX−1​(x−μ)

Henceforth we will use the notation Σ to represent CX​. Definition 1: X is multivariate Gaussian with mean vector μ and covariance matrix Σ (denoted by X∼N(μ,Σ)) if for some A and μ, it can be written as X=AZ+μ where Z is a standard normal vector and Σ=AAT.

Filling in the step between the two expressions (A square and invertible). The first expression is just the slide 9 formula with b=μ. Let v=x−μ. We need to rewrite two things in terms of Σ=AAT.

The exponent. fZ​ needs wTw with w=A−1v. Using (A−1)T=(AT)−1 and (AT)−1A−1=(AAT)−1:

(A−1v)T(A−1v)=vT(AT)−1A−1v=vT(AAT)−1v=vTΣ−1v.

The constant. detΣ=det(A)det(AT)=(detA)2, so ∣detA∣=detΣ​.

Put them together:

fX​(x)=(2π)n/2detΣ​1​exp(−21​(x−μ)TΣ−1(x−μ))​

Making sense of the formula.

  • With n=1 and Σ=σ2 you get the usual 2π​σ1​e−(x−μ)2/(2σ2). So "divide by σ2" becomes "multiply by Σ−1", and "σ" in front becomes "detΣ​".
  • The density depends on A only through Σ=AAT. Lots of different A's give the same Σ (for example A and AQ for any orthogonal Q), and they all give the same distribution. That's why writing N(μ,Σ) makes sense: a Gaussian vector is completely pinned down by its mean vector and covariance matrix.
  • The formula needs Σ invertible (detΣ>0). The degenerate case from slide 11 is still covered by Definition 1, it just has no pdf.
  • Check against L19 slide 1. X=(Z1​,Z1​+Z2​) has A=[11​01​], Σ=[11​12​], detΣ=1, Σ−1=[2−1​−11​]. The boxed formula gives 2π1​e−21​(2x12​−2x1​x2​+x22​), the same as the Jacobian answer there. ✓

Slide 13/36: Three equivalent definitions

On the slide. The following are equivalent definitions (without proof):

  1. X∼N(μ,Σ) if for some A and μ, it can be written as X=AZ+μ.
  2. X∼N(μ,Σ) if it has the pdf fX​(x)=(2π)n/2det(Σ)​1​e−21​(x−μ)TΣ−1(x−μ).
  3. X∼N(μ,Σ) iff for all vectors a∈Rn, it turns out that aTX is univariate Gaussian N(aTμ,aTΣa).

For equivalent definitions see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_normal_distribution

Three ways to say the same thing. Each one is handy for a different job:

Definition Use it to...
1. X=AZ+μ build or simulate a Gaussian vector; prove things by going back to independent Z's
2. the pdf compute probabilities and conditional densities; spot a Gaussian from the form of its density
3. every linear combination is normal check whether something is a Gaussian vector; get the distribution of any aTX instantly

Definition 3 is the one in last year's HW9 Q2 and Tutorial 9 Q3 ("X and Y are bivariate normal if aX+bY is normal for all a and b"). A constant counts as a normal with variance 0 here.

It's the most useful one in exams. For example, X1​−3X2​+X3​ is just aTX with a=(1,−3,1)T, so it's N(aTμ,aTΣa), no integrals at all.

Why they agree (sketch, not needed for the exam).

  • (1 ⇒ 3) aTX=(ATa)TZ+aTμ is a linear combination of independent normals plus a constant, so it's normal (L14 slide 5, via MGFs). Mean and variance from L19.
  • (1 ⇒ 2) That's slide 12, when A is invertible.
  • (2 ⇒ 1) Take A=Σ1/2 (the symmetric square root), and use the Jacobian to check that Z=A−1(X−μ) has the pdf from slide 10.
  • (3 ⇒ 1) If every sTX is normal, the multivariate MGF is E[esTX]=esTμ+21​sTΣs (slide 14). That's also the MGF of AZ+μ for any A with AAT=Σ. Same MGF, same distribution.

Slide 14/36: Affine maps preserve Gaussianity

On the slide. Suppose X∼N(μ,Σ); then what can we say about Y=AX+b? Is it a Gaussian vector? Easy to see that E[Y]=AE[X]+b and CY​=AΣAT. Like in the univariate case, we can use MGF (for multivariate MGF see Bertsekas) to show the following. Suppose X∼N(μ,Σ). Now consider Y=AX+b. Then we have Y∼N(AE[X]+b,AΣAT).

X∼N(μ,Σ) ⟹ AX+b∼N(Aμ+b, AΣAT)​

The mean and covariance are free from L19. What's new is that Y is still Gaussian. (Quick intuition with Definition 1: X=A′Z+μ, so AX+b=(AA′)Z+(Aμ+b), which is again "matrix times Z plus a shift".) Here's the MGF proof the slide mentions. It's last year's HW9 Q10 and Tutorial 9 Q4.

The multivariate MGF. For a random vector, MX​(s)=E[esTX] for s∈Rn. Same as in L14: if it's finite near s=0, it determines the joint distribution (Bertsekas Section 4.4).

Step 1 (HW9 Q10): the MGF of N(μ,Σ). Write X=AZ+μ and let u=ATs. Then sTX=sTAZ+sTμ=uTZ+sTμ. The Zi​ are independent, and the 1D normal MGF is E[euZ]=eu2/2:

MX​(s)=esTμi∏​E[eui​Zi​]=esTμe21​∑i​ui2​=esTμ+21​uTu.

And uTu=sTAATs=sTΣs, so

MX​(s)=exp(sTμ+21​sTΣs)​

That's the 1D formula eμt+σ2t2/2 with t swapped for the vector s.

Step 2 (Tutorial 9 Q4): the MGF of Y=AX+b. Since sTY=(ATs)TX+sTb, just evaluate Step 1 at ATs:

MY​(s)=esTbMX​(ATs)=exp(sT(Aμ+b)+21​sT(AΣAT)s).

That's exactly the MGF of N(Aμ+b,AΣAT), so by uniqueness that's the distribution of Y. □

A can be any m×n matrix here. Two special choices give useful things:

  • A = a single row aT: that's Definition 3 from slide 13.
  • A = a matrix that picks out some coordinates: that's the marginal property on the next slide.

Slide 15/36: Marginalization and conditioning

On the slide. Let X∼N(μ,Σ) and partition X as [X1​,X2​]T, where X1​ is m×1 and X2​ is (n−m)×1. We similarly have μ=[μ1​,μ2​]T and Σ=[Σ11​Σ21​​Σ12​Σ22​​], where Σ11​ is an m×m matrix and so on. Marginalization property: the m-dimensional marginal distribution of X1​ is N(μ1​,Σ11​) and X2​ is N(μ2​,Σ22​). Conditioning property: the m-dimensional conditional distribution of X1​ given X2​=x2​ is

N(μ1​+Σ12​Σ22−1​(x2​−μ2​), Σ11​−Σ12​Σ22−1​Σ21​).

Note the decrease in variance, which does not depend on x2​.

Setup: split the vector into two chunks, X1​ (what we care about) and X2​ (the rest), and split μ and Σ the same way. Σ11​ is the covariance within chunk 1, Σ22​ within chunk 2, and Σ12​=Σ21T​ is the cross-covariance between them.

The slide gives no proof. Here are both, since the second one is last year's Tutorial 9 Q6.

Marginalization. X1​=[Im​  0]X (a matrix that keeps the first m coordinates and throws away the rest). By slide 14 it's Gaussian with

mean [Im​  0]μ=μ1​,covariance [Im​  0]Σ[Im​  0]T=Σ11​.

In words: to get a marginal, just delete the rows and columns of the variables you don't want. No integrals.

For example, if X∼N(μ,Σ) in R3: writing σij​ for the entries of the 3×3 matrix Σ, X2​∼N(μ2​,σ22​), and (X1​,X3​) has mean (μ1​,μ3​) and covariance [σ11​σ31​​σ13​σ33​​].

Conditioning: the "remove what X2​ explains" proof. The plan: split X1​ into a part that's a function of X2​, plus a leftover that's independent of X2​. Then conditioning is easy. Let B=Σ12​Σ22−1​ and define the leftover (residual)

W=X1​−BX2​.
  1. (W,X2​) is a Gaussian vector, because it's a linear function of X (slide 14).
  2. W and X2​ are uncorrelated. That's exactly what B was chosen for:
Cov(W,X2​)=Cov(X1​,X2​)−BCov(X2​,X2​)=Σ12​−Σ12​Σ22−1​Σ22​=0.
  1. So they're independent. For a Gaussian vector, zero cross-covariance makes the MGF split into a product. With a block-diagonal covariance,
exp(s1T​μW​+s2T​μ2​+21​s1T​ΣW​s1​+21​s2T​Σ22​s2​)=MW​(s1​)MX2​​(s2​),

which is the MGF of an independent pair. 4. Mean and covariance of W. E[W]=μ1​−Bμ2​. Expanding Cov(X1​−BX2​):

ΣW​=Σ11​−BΣ21​−Σ12​BT+BΣ22​BT=Σ11​−Σ12​Σ22−1​Σ21​.

(Each of the last three terms equals Σ12​Σ22−1​Σ21​, using Σ21​=Σ12T​ and Σ22​ symmetric. Two minus signs and one plus leave one minus.) 5. Now condition. X1​=W+BX2​. Given X2​=x2​, the piece Bx2​ is just a constant, and W doesn't care (it's independent of X2​). So

X1​∣X2​=x2​ ∼ N(μ1​−Bμ2​+Bx2​, ΣW​)=N(μ1​+Σ12​Σ22−1​(x2​−μ2​), Σ11​−Σ12​Σ22−1​Σ21​). □

Making sense of the formula.

  • The conditional mean is linear in x2​. Start at μ1​, then move by Σ12​Σ22−1​ times the "surprise" x2​−μ2​. With one variable in each chunk it's μ1​+σ22​σ12​​(x2​−μ2​), a straight line in x2​ (the regression line).
  • The conditional covariance is smaller, since we subtract the PSD matrix Σ12​Σ22−1​Σ21​. Seeing X2​ reduces our uncertainty about X1​.
  • The slide's note: the reduction is the same no matter which value x2​ we see. That's special to Gaussians. For most other joint distributions the conditional variance depends on the observed value.
  • If Σ12​=0, then X1​∣X2​∼N(μ1​,Σ11​), which is just the marginal. So uncorrelated parts of a Gaussian vector are independent.

Slide 16/36: Towards bivariate Gaussians

On the slide. Suppose X1​∼N(μ1​,σ12​) and X2​∼N(μ2​,σ22​). Also suppose X1​ and X2​ are independent. For x=[x1​,x2​]T [the slide prints [x2​,x2​]T], we have

fX​(x)=fX1​​(x1​)fX2​​(x2​)=2πσ1​σ2​1​e−(2σ12​(x1​−μ1​)2​+2σ22​(x2​−μ2​)2​)=(2π)det(Σ)​1​e−21​(x−μ)TΣ−1(x−μ)

where Σ=[σ12​0​0σ22​​], and hence X is bivariate Gaussian. In general, a vector composed of independent Gaussians is a Gaussian vector. The converse is not true: a vector of dependent Gaussian components need not be a Gaussian vector (EX 5.35 in probabilitycourse.com).

Checking the last equality. With a diagonal Σ everything is easy. detΣ=σ12​σ22​, so detΣ​=σ1​σ2​. And Σ−1=diag(1/σ12​,1/σ22​), so

21​(x−μ)TΣ−1(x−μ)=2σ12​(x1​−μ1​)2​+2σ22​(x2​−μ2​)2​. ✓

That matches the slide-13 pdf with n=2, so X is a Gaussian vector.

The counterexample: each component Gaussian, but not a Gaussian vector (probabilitycourse 5.3.2; the slide calls it EX 5.35). Let X∼N(0,1), and independently flip a fair coin W. Set Y=X on heads, Y=−X on tails.

  • Y∼N(0,1). Condition on the coin: FY​(y)=21​Φ(y)+21​P(−X≤y)=21​Φ(y)+21​Φ(y)=Φ(y), since −X∼N(0,1) too. So each component is normal.
  • But (X,Y) is not a Gaussian vector. X+Y is 2X on heads and 0 on tails, so P(X+Y=0)=21​. A normal with positive variance gives probability 0 to any single point, and X+Y isn't a constant either. So X+Y isn't normal, and Definition 3 fails with a=(1,1).
  • And they're uncorrelated: Cov(X,Y)=E[XY]=21​E[X2]−21​E[X2]=0. Yet they're obviously dependent, since ∣Y∣=∣X∣ always.

The lesson: "uncorrelated implies independent" holds for jointly Gaussian variables (slide 15). It does not hold for variables that just happen to each be Gaussian on their own. Exam questions test exactly this.

Slide 17/36: Bivariate Gaussians

On the slide. In general, X1​ and X2​ need not be independent, in which case we have a general bivariate Gaussian X=[X1​,X2​]T∼N(μ,Σ), where μ=[μ1​,μ2​]T and Σ=[σ11​σ21​​σ12​σ22​​]. Show that bivariate Gaussian is closed under marginalization, i.e., X1​∼N(μ1​,σ11​) and X2​∼N(μ2​,σ22​). Show that bivariate Gaussian is closed under conditioning (for proof see Theorem 5.4, probabilitycourse.com). This means that given X2​=x2​, one can show that fX1​∣X2​​(x1​∣x2​) is Gaussian. These two properties make multivariate Gaussians efficient modelling tools and handy in Gaussian processes and Bayesian optimization.

The bivariate density written out. Use the usual parameters: σ11​=σ12​, σ22​=σ22​, and σ12​=σ21​=ρσ1​σ2​, where ρ∈(−1,1) is the correlation. Then

detΣ=σ12​σ22​−ρ2σ12​σ22​=σ12​σ22​(1−ρ2),Σ−1=σ12​σ22​(1−ρ2)1​[σ22​−ρσ1​σ2​​−ρσ1​σ2​σ12​​]

(the 2×2 inverse rule: swap the diagonal, flip the sign of the off-diagonal, divide by the determinant). Write the standardised values u=σ1​x1​−μ1​​ and v=σ2​x2​−μ2​​. The slide-13 pdf becomes

f(x1​,x2​)=2πσ1​σ2​1−ρ2​1​exp(−2(1−ρ2)u2−2ρuv+v2​)​

With μ=0 and σ1​=σ2​=1 it's the formula quoted in last year's HW9 Q2 and Tutorial 9 Q3.

Both red questions at once: complete the square. The trick is

u2−2ρuv+v2=(1−ρ2)u2+(v−ρu)2

(expand the right side to check). Plug it in and the exponential splits into two pieces:

f(x1​,x2​)=pdf of N(μ1​,σ12​) at x1​2π​σ1​1​e−u2/2​​ × pdf of N(μ2​+ρσ2​u, (1−ρ2)σ22​) at x2​2π​σ2​1−ρ2​1​exp(−2(1−ρ2)(v−ρu)2​)​​.

(Check the second piece: 1−ρ2(v−ρu)2​=(1−ρ2)σ22​(x2​−μ2​−ρσ2​u)2​, which is the exponent of that normal.)

  • Marginal. Integrate over x2​. The second piece is a pdf in x2​, so it integrates to 1. What's left is fX1​​(x1​) = the N(μ1​,σ12​) pdf. So X1​∼N(μ1​,σ11​). By symmetry (complete the square in u instead), X2​∼N(μ2​,σ22​).
  • Conditional. fX2​∣X1​​(x2​∣x1​)=fX1​​(x1​)f(x1​,x2​)​, which is exactly the second piece:
X2​∣X1​=x1​ ∼ N(μ2​+ρσ2​σ1​x1​−μ1​​, (1−ρ2)σ22​)(probabilitycourse Theorem 5.4).

Swapping the roles of the two variables:

X1​∣X2​=x2​ ∼ N(μ1​+ρσ1​σ2​x2​−μ2​​, (1−ρ2)σ12​)​

Same as slide 15 with Σ12​Σ22−1​=σ22​ρσ1​σ2​​=σ2​ρσ1​​ and Σ11​−Σ22​Σ122​​=σ12​−ρ2σ12​. ✓

How to remember the conditional. Think in standard units. If X2​ is v SDs above its mean, the best guess for X1​ is ρv SDs above its mean. Since ∣ρ∣<1, the guess is pulled back towards the mean ("regression to the mean"). The leftover spread is σ1​1−ρ2​. At ρ=0, seeing X2​ tells you nothing. As ∣ρ∣→1, it tells you almost everything.

The constructive view (probabilitycourse 5.3.2, Theorem 5.3). Every bivariate normal can be built as

X1​=μ1​+σ1​Z1​,X2​=μ2​+σ2​(ρZ1​+1−ρ2​Z2​),

with Z1​,Z2​ independent N(0,1). That's Definition 1 with A=[σ1​ρσ2​​0σ2​1−ρ2​​]; multiply out to check AAT=Σ.

This is the usual way to answer Tutorial 9 Q3: the pair has the right means, variances and correlation, every aX1​+bX2​ is normal, and a Gaussian vector is fixed by its mean and covariance. The Jacobian (in standard units, Z1​=U, Z2​=1−ρ2​V−ρU​, so ∣J∣=1−ρ2​1​) then gives the boxed pdf.

Gaussian processes and Bayesian optimisation (just context, not exam material). A Gaussian process says: the values of an unknown function at any finite set of points form a Gaussian vector. Once you know the function at a few points, slide 15's conditioning formula gives, in closed form, a best guess (conditional mean) and an uncertainty (conditional variance) at every other point. Bayesian optimisation uses those to decide where to look next. Both only need the two closure properties on this slide.

Slides 18 and 19/36: Pictures of bivariate Gaussian pdfs

On the slides. Slide 18: a 3-D plot of a bell-shaped joint density p(x,y) over the (x,y) plane, with the two marginal densities p(x) and p(y) drawn as curves on the back walls. Slide 19: a cloud of simulated points from a bivariate Gaussian, with a green ellipse around the bulk of the cloud, and histograms of each coordinate on the back walls with the marginal pdfs (red and blue curves) drawn over them.

What to notice.

  1. The marginals are normal curves (slide 17's marginal property), on both slides. On slide 19 the histograms of each coordinate match the normal curves drawn on top.
  2. The marginal curves can have different heights. A normal pdf peaks at 2π​σ1​, so the taller, narrower one is the coordinate with the smaller variance.
  3. The contours are ellipses. The density is constant where (x−μ)TΣ−1(x−μ)=c, which is an ellipse centred at μ, like the green curve on slide 19.
    • ρ=0: the ellipse's axes line up with the coordinate axes (and it's a circle if also σ1​=σ2​).
    • ρ=0: it's tilted. ρ>0 leans along a rising line, ρ<0 along a falling one.
    • In general the axes point along the eigenvectors of Σ, with half-lengths proportional to the square roots of the eigenvalues.
  4. How much probability is inside an ellipse? B12 works it out: the "2-SD" ellipse (c=4) holds only about 86%, not the 95% you'd guess from the 1D rule.

Part B: extra worked examples and problems

General plan.

  • Distribution of any linear combination aTX: it's N(aTμ,aTΣa). Then standardise and use Φ.
  • Marginal: delete rows and columns.
  • Conditional: slide 15 (general) or slide 17 (two variables).
  • Independence inside a Gaussian vector: just check covariance = 0.
  • "Is this a Gaussian vector?": try to write it as AZ+μ (yes), or find a linear combination that isn't normal (no).

B1 (last year's HW9 Q4). X∼N(m,C) with m=[12​], C=[41​11​]. Let Y=AX+b with A=​2−11​113​​ and b=​−101​​. Find (a) P(X2​>0), (b) mY​, (c) CY​, (d) P(Y2​≤2).

Solution

Solution. (a) Marginal: X2​∼N(2,1) (second entry of m, bottom-right of C). So

P(X2​>0)=P(Z>10−2​)=P(Z>−2)=Φ(2)≈0.9772.

(b) mY​=Am+b=(2+2, −1+2, 1+6)+(−1,0,1)=(3,1,8)T. (c) Two steps:

AC=​9−37​304​​,CY​=ACAT=​21−618​−63−3​18−319​​.

(d) Y2​=−X1​+X2​ (plus b2​=0). From (b) and (c), Y2​∼N(1,3). So

P(Y2​≤2)=Φ(3​2−1​)=Φ(0.577)≈0.7181.

Side remark. Y has 3 components but is built from the 2-dimensional X, so CY​ is singular (detCY​=0). It's a degenerate Gaussian with no pdf in R3, even though every single component is a perfectly normal variable (slide 11).

B2 (last year's HW9 Q5). X=(X1​,X2​,X3​)∼N(μ,Σ) with μ=(1,2,3)T and Σ=​410​121​013​​. Find the distribution of (X1​,X3​) given X2​=x2​.

Solution

Solution. Chunk 1 = (X1​,X3​) (what we want), chunk 2 = X2​ (what we observe). Read off the right entries:

Σ11​=[σ11​σ31​​σ13​σ33​​]=[40​03​],Σ12​=[Cov(X1​,X2​)Cov(X3​,X2​)​]=[11​],Σ22​=2.

So Σ12​Σ22−1​=[1/21/2​], and plugging into slide 15:

μ1∣2​=[13​]+2x2​−2​[11​],Σ1∣2​=[40​03​]−21​[11​11​]=[3.5−0.5​−0.52.5​].

Notice. X1​ and X3​ start out uncorrelated (so independent), but given X2​ they're negatively correlated. Both are positively linked to X2​. Once X2​ is fixed, a high X1​ already "accounts for" some of X2​'s value, which suggests a lower X3​.

B3 (last year's HW9 Q6): a degenerate Gaussian. Z=(Z1​,Z2​)∼N(m,C) with m=(1,2)T and C=[2−1​−13​]. Let W=AZ+b with A=​112​1−10​​, b=(0,0,−2)T. (a) Find the mean and covariance of W. (b) Find P(W2​>1).

Solution

Solution. (Careful: here Z isn't standard normal, it's just what the vector is called.) (a) E[W]=Am+b=(3,−1,2)+(0,0,−2)=(3,−1,0)T. Then

AC=​134​2−4−2​​,CW​=ACAT=​3−12​−176​268​​.

Spot checks: Var(W2​)=Var(Z1​−Z2​)=2+3−2(−1)=7 and Var(W3​)=Var(2Z1​)=4⋅2=8. ✓ Like B1, detCW​=0 (rank 2). (b) W2​∼N(−1,7), so

P(W2​>1)=1−Φ(7​1−(−1)​)=1−Φ(0.756)≈0.2248.

B4 (last year's HW9 Q2). (X,Y) is standard bivariate normal with correlation ρ (pdf in slide 17). Find the joint pdf of U=X+Y and V=X−Y.

Solution 1 (the fast way, slide 14). (U,V) is a linear function of a Gaussian vector, so it's Gaussian. Mean 0. Covariance:

Var(U)=1+1+2ρ=2+2ρ,Var(V)=2−2ρ,Cov(U,V)=Var(X)−Var(Y)=0.

Uncorrelated parts of a Gaussian vector are independent, so U∼N(0,2(1+ρ)) and V∼N(0,2(1−ρ)), independent. Multiply the two densities:

fU,V​(u,v)=4π1−ρ2​1​exp(−4(1+ρ)u2​−4(1−ρ)v2​).

(The constant: 2(1+ρ)⋅2(1−ρ)​=21−ρ2​, times 2π.)

Solution 2 (the Jacobian, L19). x=2u+v​, y=2u−v​, ∣J∣=21​, and

x2−2ρxy+y2=2(1−ρ)u2+(1+ρ)v2​.

Plug into the pdf and you get the same answer. More algebra, same result, so use Solution 1.

B5 (last year's HW9 Q11). X is a standard normal vector in Rn and Y=AX+b, with A square, symmetric and invertible. (a) Find fY​. (b) Evaluate it for A=[20​03​], b=(1,−1)T, y=(3,2)T.

Solution

Solution. (a) Slide 12 with Σ=AAT=A2 (A symmetric), so Σ−1=A−2 and detΣ​=∣detA∣:

fY​(y)=(2π)n/2∣detA∣1​exp(−21​(y−b)TA−2(y−b))=(2π)n/2∣detA∣1​exp(−21​​A−1(y−b)​2).

(b) y−b=(2,3), so A−1(y−b)=(22​,33​)=(1,1), with squared length 2. detA=6. So

fY​(y)=2π⋅61​e−1=12πe−1​≈0.00976.

B6 (last year's Tutorial 9 Q5). X∼N(0,[52​21​]). Find a such that Y1​=X1​+aX2​ and Y2​=X2​ are independent.

Solution

Solution. (Y1​,Y2​) is a linear image of X, so it's Gaussian, and independence is the same as zero covariance:

Cov(X1​+aX2​,X2​)=Cov(X1​,X2​)+aVar(X2​)=2+a=0⟹a=−2.

In general a=−σ22​σ12​​, and Y1​ is exactly the residual W from the slide-15 proof.

Bonus: Var(Y1​)=5+4⋅1−2⋅2⋅2=1, and X1​=Y1​+2X2​. So X1​∣X2​=x2​∼N(2x2​,1), just like the conditioning formula says.

B7 (probabilitycourse 5.3.2, numerical example). X,Y are bivariate normal with μX​=1, σX2​=1, μY​=0, σY2​=4, ρ=21​. Find (a) P(2X+Y≤3), (b) Cov(X+Y,2X−Y), (c) P(Y>1∣X=2).

Solution

Solution. First, Cov(X,Y)=ρσX​σY​=21​⋅1⋅2=1. (a) V=2X+Y is normal (linear combination), mean 2⋅1+0=2, variance 4⋅1+4+2⋅2⋅1=12. So

P(V≤3)=Φ(12​3−2​)≈0.6136.

(b) Expand by bilinearity, term by term:

Cov(X+Y,2X−Y)=2Var(X)−Cov(X,Y)+2Cov(Y,X)−Var(Y)=2−1+2−4=−1.

(c) Slide 17 with the roles set as Y given X: mean 0+ρσY​σX​2−1​=21​⋅2⋅1=1, variance (1−41​)⋅4=3. So

P(Y>1∣X=2)=1−Φ(0)=21​.

(The threshold 1 is exactly the conditional mean, so it's a coin flip.)

B8 (Bertsekas Chapter 4, Problem 28): the bivariate normal from scratch. The zero-mean bivariate normal pdf is f(x,y)=ce−q(x,y) with

q(x,y)=2(1−ρ2)σx2​x2​−2ρσx​σy​xy​+σy2​y2​​,−1<ρ<1.

(a) Write q as (αx−βy)2+γ2y2. (b) Show X∼N(0,σx2​) and Y∼N(0,σy2​). (c) Find c. (d) Find the conditional pdf of X given Y=y. (e) Show the correlation coefficient is ρ. (f) Show X,Y are independent iff uncorrelated. (g) Show the estimation error E[X∣Y]−X is normal with mean 0 and variance (1−ρ2)σx2​, and independent of Y.

Solution

Solution. This is slide 17 again, done by hand. (a) Complete the square in x (same trick as slide 17):

q=2(1−ρ2)(σx​x​−ρσy​y​)2​+2σy2​y2​,soα=σx​2(1−ρ2)​1​,  β=σy​2(1−ρ2)​ρ​,  γ=2​σy​1​.

(b) For fixed y, ∫e−(αx−βy)2dx=απ​​ (a Gaussian integral; shifting by βy doesn't change it). So

fY​(y)=ce−γ2y2⋅απ​​=αcπ​​e−y2/(2σy2​),

a N(0,σy2​) shape. By symmetry, X∼N(0,σx2​). (c) Match fY​ with 2π​σy​1​e−y2/(2σy2​):

c=π​2π​σy​α​=2πσx​σy​1−ρ2​1​.

(d) Divide by fY​: what's left, as a function of x, is

fX∣Y​(x∣y)∝e−(αx−βy)2=exp(−2(1−ρ2)σx2​(x−ρσy​σx​​y)2​),

so X∣Y=y∼N(ρσy​σx​​y, (1−ρ2)σx2​). (e) Use iterated expectation with (d):

E[XY]=E[YE[X∣Y]]=ρσy​σx​​E[Y2]=ρσy​σx​​σy2​=ρσx​σy​.

Both means are 0, so this is the covariance, and the correlation coefficient is σx​σy​ρσx​σy​​=ρ. (f) Independent always implies uncorrelated. Conversely, uncorrelated means ρ=0, and then q=2σx2​x2​+2σy2​y2​, so the pdf splits into an x part times a y part. (g) Given Y=y, the error is ρσy​σx​​y−X, which by (d) is N(0,(1−ρ2)σx2​), whatever y is. Its conditional distribution doesn't depend on y, so the error is independent of Y, and that's also its unconditional distribution.

B9 (conditioning with numbers). (X1​,X2​) is bivariate normal with μ1​=170, σ1​=7, μ2​=175, σ2​=8, ρ=0.5. Find P(X1​>180∣X2​=183), and compare it with P(X1​>180).

Solution

Solution. By slide 17, X1​∣X2​=183 is normal with

mean 170+0.5⋅87​(183−175)=170+3.5=173.5,SD 71−0.25​≈6.062.

So

P(X1​>180∣X2​=183)=1−Φ(6.062180−173.5​)=1−Φ(1.072)≈0.142.

Without conditioning, P(X1​>180)=1−Φ(10/7)≈0.077. So the information almost doubles the chance.

Notice: X2​=183 is exactly 1 SD above its mean, and the prediction for X1​ moves only ρ×1=0.5 SD above its mean (that's the +3.5). Regression to the mean in action.

B10: simulating any bivariate normal (probabilitycourse 5.3.2, Eq. 5.23, plus Box–Muller from L19 B11).

  1. Make Z1​,Z2​ independent N(0,1) from two uniforms with Box–Muller.
  2. Find A with AAT=Σ. For 2×2, the lower-triangular one (the Cholesky factor) is A=[σ1​ρσ2​​0σ2​1−ρ2​​].
  3. Output X=AZ+μ (Definition 1).

Example. Σ=[42​25​]. Then σ1​=2, ρσ2​=σ1​σ12​​=1, and σ2​1−ρ2​=σ22​−(ρσ2​)2​=5−1​=2. So A=[21​02​]; check AAT=[42​25​]. ✓ With μ=(1,0) and Z=(0.5,−1), the sample is X=(1+2⋅0.5, 0+0.5−2)=(2,−1.5).

In code, any dimension:

import numpy as np
L = np.linalg.cholesky(Sigma)            # lower triangular, L @ L.T == Sigma
Z = np.random.standard_normal((N, len(mu)))
X = mu + Z @ L.T                         # each row is one sample of N(mu, Sigma)
print(np.cov(X, rowvar=False))           # close to Sigma for large N

B11: Gaussian vector or not? X,Z are independent N(0,1). Decide for each pair.

  1. (X,3X+1). Yes, Definition 1 with A=[1,3]T and shift (0,1). But degenerate: everything sits on the line y=3x+1, so no joint pdf.
  2. (X+Z,X−Z). Yes, a linear image of the standard normal vector (X,Z). In fact two independent N(0,2)'s (B4 with ρ=0).
  3. (X,Y) with Y=±X on a fair coin flip. No (slide 16).
  4. (X,Y) with Y=∣Z∣sign(X). No. Y on its own is N(0,1), because ∣Z∣ gets a random sign that's independent of it. But X and Y always have the same sign, so P(X>0,Y<0)=0. Why that rules it out: a non-degenerate bivariate normal has a positive pdf everywhere, so it gives every quadrant positive probability. A degenerate one lives on a line through the origin, Y=cX, but here, given X, Y is still random. Neither case fits.
  5. (X,X2). No. X2 isn't even normal.

B12: how much probability is inside an ellipse? Let X∼N(μ,Σ) in R2 with Σ invertible. Find P((X−μ)TΣ−1(X−μ)≤c).

Solution

Solution. Write X=AZ+μ. The slide-12 calculation showed the quadratic form equals ZTZ=Z12​+Z22​. So the question is really about Z12​+Z22​.

By Box–Muller (L19 B11), Z12​+Z22​=R2=−2lnU for a uniform U. So

P(Z12​+Z22​≤c)=P(−2lnU≤c)=P(U≥e−c/2)=1−e−c/2,

i.e. Z12​+Z22​∼ Exponential with rate 21​.

  • "2-SD ellipse" (c=4): 1−e−2≈0.865, not 95%.
  • The ellipse holding 95%: 1−e−c/2=0.95, so c=−2ln0.05≈5.99.

(In n dimensions, ZTZ has the chi-square distribution with n degrees of freedom. You'll see it again in statistics.)
